questions.stem: Find the value of $3^4$.
questions.hint: An exponent tells you how many times to multiply the base by itself: $3^4 = 3 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3$.

steps.explain: Write out the power as a repeated multiplication.
Multiply step-by-step.

questions.stem: Find the value of $3 \times 4^3$.
questions.hint: According to BODMAS, exponents (orders) must be calculated before multiplication: calculate $4^3$ first.

steps.explain: Evaluate the exponent \(4^3\) first.
Multiply the result by \(3\).

questions.stem: Write the exponential expression as an ordinary number:\n\\(2 \\times 5^3\\)
questions.hint: Order of operations applies: calculate the power first (5^3), then multiply by 2.
questions.solution:
Calculate step-by-step:
1. Evaluate power first: \\(5^3 = 5 \\times 5 \\times 5 = 125\\).
2. Multiply: \\(2 \\times 125 = 250\\).

steps.explain: Determine the value of the exponential term first according to order of operations.
Multiply the resulting value by 2.
Compute the final product.

questions.stem: Buzz: take turns to count by ones, going around the class. When you get to a number that is a multiple of the given number, say 'buzz'. Start at 0, buzz on multiples of 3. Which list shows the first 10 numbers (after 0) you buzz on?
questions.hint: Start at 3 and add 3 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 3s, starting at 3. So we start at 3 and add 3 each time.

Why the other answers are wrong: one list leaves out the starting number, another uses the wrong jump size, and another counts in the opposite direction.

keyPoints.note: The starting number is the first number in the list.
Skip-count by the number to list its multiples.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 3: Multiples and factors

questions.stem: Buzz: take turns to count by ones, going around the class. When you get to a number that is a multiple of the given number, say 'buzz'. Start at 0, buzz on multiples of 7. Which list shows the first 10 numbers (after 0) you buzz on?
questions.hint: Start at 7 and add 7 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 7s, starting at 7. So we start at 7 and add 7 each time.

questions.stem: Buzz: take turns to count by ones, going around the class. When you get to a number that is a multiple of the given number, say 'buzz'. Start at 0, buzz on multiples of 4. Which list shows the first 10 numbers (after 0) you buzz on?
questions.hint: Start at 4 and add 4 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

questions.stem: Buzz: take turns to count by ones, going around the class. When you get to a number that is a multiple of the given number, say 'buzz'. Start at 0, buzz on multiples of 11. Which list shows the first 10 numbers (after 0) you buzz on?
questions.hint: Start at 11 and add 11 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 11s, starting at 11. So we start at 11 and add 11 each time.

questions.stem: Take turns making up fun multiples of 2, 10 or 5. For example, the number nine eight seven six five four three two one zero (9 876 543 210). Of the numbers 2, 5 and 10, which is it a multiple of?
questions.hint: Look at the LAST digit only: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 gives multiples of 2; 0 or 5 gives multiples of 5; 0 gives multiples of 10.

steps.explain: Only the last digit matters for 2, 5 and 10, so look at the last digit of the number.
Multiples of 2 end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5. Multiples of 10 end in 0.
It ends in 0. Every number that ends in 0 is a multiple of 10, and a multiple of 10 is also a multiple of 2 and of 5.
Why the other answers are wrong: each of them tests a different last digit from the one the number really has.

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

steps.explain: Only the last digit matters for 2, 5 and 10, so look at the last digit of the number.
Multiples of 2 end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5. Multiples of 10 end in 0.
It ends in 2. Numbers ending in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 are multiples of 2. It does not end in 0 or 5, so it is not a multiple of 5 or 10.

questions.hint: Look at the LAST digit only: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 gives multiples of 2; 0 or 5 gives multiples of 5; 0 gives multiples of 10.

steps.explain: Only the last digit matters for 2, 5 and 10, so look at the last digit of the number.
Multiples of 2 end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5. Multiples of 10 end in 0.
It ends in 5. Numbers ending in 0 or 5 are multiples of 5. It is odd, so it is not a multiple of 2, and it does not end in 0, so it is not a multiple of 10.
Why the other answers are wrong: each of them tests a different last digit from the one the number really has.

questions.hint: 2 × 9 is 2 rows of 9. Two lots of it fill the whole diagram in two equal halves.

steps.explain: '2 × 9' is 2 rows of 9 squares (18 squares). 2 lots of that is 2 × 2 × 9 = 36 squares, which is the whole diagram.
So the diagram is split into TWO equal parts of 2 rows each, shaded in two different colours.

questions.hint: Find the number of groups, then the shape of each group. Check the total is 24.

steps.explain: Read the words: the first number is the number of GROUPS (lots); the rest tells how each group is arranged (rows × counters in each row).
Work out how many counters one group has, then multiply by the number of groups. The total must be 24.

questions.hint: Find the number of groups, then the shape of each group. Check the total is 24.

steps.explain: Read the words: the first number is the number of GROUPS (lots); the rest tells how each group is arranged (rows × counters in each row).
Work out how many counters one group has, then multiply by the number of groups. The total must be 24.

questions.stem: Copy and complete the first 12 multiples of 5. Say '1 five is 5', '2 fives are 10', and so on, as you complete each one. Check your answers by counting in fives. 7 × 5 = ____
questions.hint: Think of 7 groups of 5: skip-count in 5s, 7 times, or use a table you know.

steps.explain: Read the problem as equal groups: 7 rows with 5 in each row (or 7 groups of 5). The total is found by multiplying.

questions.stem: Copy and complete the first 12 multiples of 5. Say '1 five is 5', '2 fives are 10', and so on, as you complete each one. Check your answers by counting in fives. 10 × 5 = ____

Check by swapping the order of the numbers (multiplication works either way round).

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 3: Multiples and factors

questions.stem: Copy and complete the first 12 multiples of 5. Say '1 five is 5', '2 fives are 10', and so on, as you complete each one. Check your answers by counting in fives. 11 × 5 = ____
questions.hint: Think of 11 groups of 5: skip-count in 5s, 11 times, or use a table you know.

steps.explain: Read the problem as equal groups: 11 rows with 5 in each row (or 11 groups of 5). The total is found by multiplying.

Check by swapping the order of the numbers (multiplication works either way round).

questions.stem: Copy and complete the first 12 multiples of 5. Say '1 five is 5', '2 fives are 10', and so on, as you complete each one. Check your answers by counting in fives. 12 × 5 = ____
questions.hint: Think of 12 groups of 5: skip-count in 5s, 12 times, or use a table you know.

steps.explain: Read the problem as equal groups: 12 rows with 5 in each row (or 12 groups of 5). The total is found by multiplying.

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).

questions.stem: Write the first 12 multiples of 7, without looking at a multiplication table. Skip-count by seven to check your answers.
questions.hint: Start at 7 and add 7 each time. The starting number is the FIRST number in the list.

steps.explain: Read the question: counting forwards (the numbers get bigger) by 7s, starting at 7. So we start at 7 and add 7 each time.

steps.explain: Use the 5-times table and add on: 6=5+1, so 6×9=5×9 + 1×9.
So the total is 54.
Check by swapping the order of the numbers (multiplication works either way round).

Check by swapping the order of the numbers (multiplication works either way round).

questions.stem: Solve this problem mentally. Yasmin buys Yummy Sourdrops in large jars of 582 sourdrops. She packs them into bags of 5 to sell in her milk bar. Can Yasmin pack all of her sourdrops in bags of 5 without having any left over? Explain your answer.
options: Yes: 582 is an even number, so it divides by 5 exactly.
Yes: 582 has a 5 in it, so it is a multiple of 5.
No: 582 is too big to divide into bags of 5.
No: 582 ends in 2, so it is not a multiple of 5 and some sourdrops are left over.
questions.hint: A number is a multiple of 5 only if its last digit is 0 or 5.

steps.explain: Packing into bags of 5 with none left over means 582 must be a multiple of 5.
Multiples of 5 always end in 0 or 5. Look at the last digit of 582.
The last digit is 2, which is not 0 or 5, so 582 is NOT a multiple of 5.
There are 2 sourdrops left over after filling 116 bags.
Why the other answers are wrong: being even does not make a number a multiple of 5; a 5 in the middle of a number does not matter; size does not matter.

keyPoints.note: Use a quick strategy, not counting one by one.

questions.stem: Solve this problem mentally. The Terrific Toy Shop buys tennis balls in large sacks of 4760 tennis balls. It sells them in boxes of 5. Can the toy shop make up an even number of boxes of 5 with none left over? Explain your answer.
options: No: 4760 does not end in 5, so it is not a multiple of 5.
Yes: 4760 ends in 0, but 5 × 951 = 4755 gives an odd number of boxes.
Yes: 4760 ends in 0 so it is a multiple of 10 (and of 5), which gives 952 boxes of 5, an even number.
questions.hint: Last digit 0 means a multiple of 5 and of 10. Then divide by 5.

steps.explain: We need 4760 to be a multiple of 5 (no left over) and 4760 ÷ 5 to be even.
4760 ends in 0, so it is a multiple of 5 (multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5).
952 ends in 2, so it is an even number.
Why the other answers are wrong: 0 is a fine last digit for multiples of 5; 4760 is even; and 5 × 951 = 4755, not 4760.

keyPoints.note: Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

questions.stem: Copy and complete each statement by using the word 'even' or 'odd'. 332 is ____.
questions.hint: Look at the last digit: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 means even; 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 means odd.

steps.explain: Only the last digit decides whether a whole number is even or odd.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8 and odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
The last digit is 2, so the number is even.
Check by sharing into 2 equal groups: 332 ÷ 2 = 166 with nothing left.
Why the other answer is wrong: it names the opposite kind of number.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers are multiples of 2? \(23,\ 35,\ 38,\ 70,\ 81\)
questions.hint: Test each number one at a time and keep only the ones that pass.

steps.explain: Test the numbers one at a time.
23 ends in 3, so it is odd (not a multiple of 2).
35 ends in 5, so it is odd (not a multiple of 2).
38 ends in 8, so it is even (a multiple of 2).
70 ends in 0, so it is even (a multiple of 2).
81 ends in 1, so it is odd (not a multiple of 2).
Collect all the numbers that passed the test.
Why the other answers are wrong: one leaves out a number that passes the test, one includes a number that fails, and one lists the numbers that FAIL.

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).

questions.stem: Write seven 9-digit numbers that are multiples of 10. Which list is correct?
questions.hint: Each number needs exactly 9 digits and must END in 0.

steps.explain: A 9-digit number is between 100 000 000 and 999 999 999. A multiple of 10 must end in 0.
Check each number in the correct list: every one has 9 digits and ends in 0.
The first wrong list has a number ending in 5 (250 000 005), so that number is not a multiple of 10.
The second wrong list has numbers with only 8 digits (for example 10 000 010).
The third wrong list has numbers ending in 5 (for example 987 654 325), which are multiples of 5 but not of 10.
Why the other answers are wrong: a list must have 9 digits and every number must end in 0.

questions.stem: Write seven 9-digit numbers that are not multiples of 10. Which list is correct?
questions.hint: Each number needs exactly 9 digits and must NOT end in 0.

steps.explain: A number is a multiple of 10 only when its last digit is 0. So 'not a multiple of 10' means the last digit is NOT 0 (the number must also have exactly 9 digits).
Every number in the correct list has 9 digits and ends in 1, 7, 3, 9, 9, 3 or 1 - never 0.
The first wrong list contains 987 654 320, which ends in 0.
The second wrong list has only 8 digits.
The third wrong list is made of multiples of 10 (every number ends in 0).
Why the other answers are wrong: one contains a multiple of 10, one has numbers with the wrong number of digits, and one is all multiples of 10.

questions.stem: Use the digits 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 to make a 5-digit number that is even and a multiple of 5. Which number does this?
questions.hint: Even and a multiple of 5 means the last digit must be 0.

steps.explain: The digits we may use are 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 - each digit only as many times as it appears (two 5s, two 0s, and one each of 6, 2, 1, 4).
62 510 has 5 digits, uses only available digits and ends in 0. A number that is a multiple of 5 and even must end in 0.
62 415 ends in 5, so it is odd (it is a multiple of 5 but not even).
6251 has only 4 digits and ends in 1.
62 513 uses a 3, which is not one of the digits.
Why the other answers are wrong: each breaks one of the conditions (a digit is not available, the wrong number of digits, or the wrong last digit).

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8.

questions.stem: Use the digits 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 to make an 8-digit number that is odd and not a multiple of 5. Which number does this?
questions.hint: Odd and not a multiple of 5 means the last digit is 1 (the only odd digit that is not 5).

steps.explain: The digits we may use are 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 - each digit only as many times as it appears (two 5s, two 0s, and one each of 6, 2, 1, 4).
65 205 041 uses all 8 digits (0, 0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6) and ends in 1: odd, and not 0 or 5, so not a multiple of 5.
65 205 045 ends in 5, so it is a multiple of 5.
65 205 040 ends in 0, so it is even.
6 520 541 has only 7 digits.
Why the other answers are wrong: each breaks one of the conditions (a digit is not available, the wrong number of digits, or the wrong last digit).

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).
Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.

questions.stem: Use the digits 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 to make a number that is a multiple of 5 and 100. Which number does this?
questions.hint: A multiple of 100 must end in 00.

steps.explain: The digits we may use are 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 - each digit only as many times as it appears (two 5s, two 0s, and one each of 6, 2, 1, 4).
25 600 uses available digits and ends in 00 - every multiple of 100 ends in 00, and 00 is also a multiple of 5.
25 650 ends in 50, so it is a multiple of 10 and 5 but not of 100.
25 605 ends in 05, so it is a multiple of 5 but not of 100.
25 060 ends in 60, so it is not a multiple of 100.
Why the other answers are wrong: each breaks one of the conditions (a digit is not available, the wrong number of digits, or the wrong last digit).

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).

questions.stem: Use the digits 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 to make three different numbers that have more than 5 digits and are multiples of 2, 5 and 10. Which list does this?
questions.hint: Each number needs 6 or more digits and must end in 0 (a multiple of 10 is also a multiple of 2 and 5).

steps.explain: The digits we may use are 5, 6, 2, 5, 0, 1, 0, 4 - each digit only as many times as it appears (two 5s, two 0s, and one each of 6, 2, 1, 4).
Each number has 6 digits (more than 5), uses available digits and ends in 0, so it is a multiple of 2, 5 and 10.
Each number in this list ends in 5, so none is even.
Each number in this list has only 5 digits.
The last number ends in 3, so it is not a multiple of 10.
Why the other answers are wrong: each breaks one of the conditions (a digit is not available, the wrong number of digits, or the wrong last digit).

questions.hint: Keep splitting off the smallest prime factor (2, 3, 5, ...) until what is left is prime.

questions.stem: Find the prime factorisation of 54.
questions.hint: Keep splitting off the smallest prime factor (2, 3, 5, ...) until what is left is prime.

steps.explain: Start with 54 and look for the SMALLEST prime that divides it. Test 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... in order.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 117.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

questions.stem: Use counters to make arrays showing that: 3, 6 and 12 are factors of 12. Which list of arrays (rows × columns) shows this?
questions.hint: Find rows × columns = 12 for each given number.

steps.explain: A number is a factor of 12 if 12 counters can be arranged in a rectangular array with that many rows (or columns) and nothing left over. We need arrays for 3, 6, 12.
3 rows of 4 counters make an array of 12 = 12 counters. So 3 (and 4) is a factor of 12.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
Rows × columns gives the total.

questions.stem: Use counters to make arrays showing that: 10, 20 and 40 are factors of 40. Which list of arrays (rows × columns) shows this?
questions.hint: Find rows × columns = 40 for each given number.

steps.explain: A number is a factor of 40 if 40 counters can be arranged in a rectangular array with that many rows (or columns) and nothing left over. We need arrays for 10, 20, 40.
10 rows of 4 counters make an array of 40 = 40 counters. So 10 (and 4) is a factor of 40.

questions.stem: 100 chart prime search: when you have finished, the numbers that have circles around them are the prime numbers less than 100. List these prime numbers.
questions.hint: Use the sieve: cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5 and 7.

steps.explain: Cross out 1 (it is not prime or composite). Circle 2, the first prime, and colour all its multiples (they are composite).
The next number not coloured is 3. Circle it and colour its multiples that are not already coloured.
Next uncoloured: 5, then 7. Circle them and colour their multiples. After 7 every composite number up to 100 has already been coloured (because 11 × 11 = 121 is bigger than 100).
The circled numbers left over are the primes less than 100.
Why the other answers are wrong: each one includes a composite number or leaves out a prime number.

keyPoints.note: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

questions.stem: 100 chart prime search: find the next prime number after 97.
questions.hint: Test 98, 99, 100, 101 in order and stop at the first prime.

steps.explain: The next prime after 97 must be bigger than 97. Test the candidates in order, smallest first.
98 = 2 × 49, so it is composite.
99 = 3 × 33, so it is composite.
100 = 2 × 50, so it is composite.
101: no prime up to its square root divides it, so 101 is prime.
101 is the first number after 97 that is prime (it is not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7, and 11 × 11 = 121 is bigger than 101).
Why the other answers are wrong: 99 = 9 × 11 and 100 = 10 × 10 are composite; 103 is prime but it is not the NEXT prime because 101 comes first.

keyPoints.note: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.

questions.stem: The numbers 12, 18, 33, 98, 196 and 333 are composite. Show this by writing each number as a product of two numbers in which no factor is 1. Which product does this for 12?
questions.hint: Find a small number (2, 3, 5, ...) that divides 12 exactly.

steps.explain: A composite number can be written as a product of two numbers that are NOT 1 and NOT the number itself.
Find a number (other than 1 and 12) that divides 12 exactly: try 2, 3, 5, ... in turn. 2 works: 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
So 12 = 2 × 6. Neither factor is 1, so 12 is composite.
Why the other answers are wrong: 12 = 1 × 12 uses the factor 1 (every number can be written that way, which does not show it is composite); the others do not multiply to 12.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A composite number has more than two factors.
A product is the answer to a multiplication.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 100.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 520.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

questions.stem: Find the prime factorisation of 280.
questions.hint: Keep splitting off the smallest prime factor (2, 3, 5, ...) until what is left is prime.

steps.explain: Start with 280 and look for the SMALLEST prime that divides it. Test 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... in order.

Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 280.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

questions.stem: Why is every prime number odd except for 2?
options: Because odd numbers cannot be divided by anything.
Because 2 is the only number that can be divided by 2.
Because every even number ends in 0.
Every even number bigger than 2 has 2 as a factor, so it has more than two factors and cannot be prime.
questions.hint: What other factor does every even number have?

steps.explain: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Every even number is a multiple of 2, so 2 is a factor of it. Take 10: its factors include 1, 2, 5 and 10.
For an even number bigger than 2, the factor 2 is NOT 1 and NOT the number itself, so there are at least three factors (1, 2 and the number): it is composite.
The number 2 itself has only the factors 1 and 2, so 2 is prime - the only even prime.
Why the other answers are wrong: odd numbers CAN be divided (by 1 and themselves, and often more); and 2 is not the only number divisible by 2; and not all even numbers end in 0.

keyPoints.note: A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.

questions.stem: Copy and complete these sentences by writing 'factor' or 'multiple'. 3 is a ____ of 27 because 27 is a ____ of 3.
questions.hint: The smaller number that divides evenly is the factor; the larger number it divides into is the multiple.

steps.explain: Remember: if a × b = c, then a and b are FACTORS of c, and c is a MULTIPLE of a and of b. The small numbers that multiply are factors; the big product is the multiple.
steps.work: \(a\times b=c\ \Rightarrow\ a,b\ \text{factors of}\ c;\ c\ \text{a multiple of}\ a,b\)

steps.explain: 27 = 9 × 3, so 3 divides 27 exactly: 3 is a factor of 27, and 27 is in the 3 times table, so it is a multiple of 3.
So the first blank is 'factor' and the second blank is 'multiple'.

Why the other answers are wrong: the two words in a statement of this kind are opposite to each other when the sentence says 'X of Y because Y is a ... of X', so 'factor, factor' and 'multiple, multiple' cannot both be right.

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).
n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 120.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

questions.hint: Keep splitting off the smallest prime factor (2, 3, 5, ...) until what is left is prime.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 444.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 261.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 7000.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

questions.stem: If it costs $6 for 3 bananas, how much does each banana cost?
questions.hint: Divide the total cost by the number of bananas.

steps.explain: The cost of 3 bananas is $6. To find the cost of ONE banana, share $6 equally between 3 bananas (divide).
Skip-count in 3s until you reach 6: 3, 6 (two jumps).

questions.stem: True or false? Sam wrote this statement in his maths book. The prime factorisation of 1140 is 1140 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 57. Is this correct? If not, what corrections does Sam need to make?
options: True: all the factors are prime.
False: 57 is not prime (57 = 3 × 19) and there is one 2 too many. It should be 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 × 19.
questions.hint: Multiply Sam's factors: do you get 1140? Is every factor prime?

steps.explain: Check whether every factor is prime. 57 is divisible by 3 (5 + 7 = 12, a multiple of 3): 57 = 3 × 19, so 57 is NOT prime.
Multiply Sam's list: 2 × 2 × 2 × 5 × 57 = 8 × 5 × 57 = 40 × 57 = 2280, which is not 1140.
Find the correct factorisation of 1140: 1140 = 2 × 570; 570 = 2 × 285; 285 = 3 × 95; 95 = 5 × 19.

Now take away the primes (31, 37, 53, 59 have only two factors).
Why the other answers are wrong: one list includes 53 (prime), one includes 34 (has an even digit 4), and one includes 61 (more than 60).

questions.stem: The sum of two prime numbers is 60. What might the numbers be?
questions.hint: Both numbers must be prime. Try pairs that add to 60 and test each number.

steps.explain: Find pairs of numbers that add to 60, then test whether BOTH are prime.
13 + 47 = 60. 13 is prime (only 1 and 13). 47 is prime (not divisible by 2, 3, 5 or 7 - and 7 × 7 = 49 > 47).
The other options add to 60 but contain a composite number: 15 = 3 × 5 and 45 = 5 × 9; 9 = 3 × 3 and 51 = 3 × 17; 20 and 40 are even and bigger than 2.
Why the other answers are wrong: they add to 60 but at least one of the numbers is not prime.

questions.stem: Write down the first 12 multiples of 4. Then complete a to l. To fill in the blanks, say '1 four is 4', '2 fours are 8', and so on. Count in fours to check your answers. 10 × 4 = ____
questions.hint: Think of 10 groups of 4: skip-count in 4s, 10 times, or use a table you know.

steps.explain: Read the problem as equal groups: 10 rows with 4 in each row (or 10 groups of 4). The total is found by multiplying.

questions.stem: Write down the first 12 multiples of 4. Then complete a to l. To fill in the blanks, say '1 four is 4', '2 fours are 8', and so on. Count in fours to check your answers. 11 × 4 = ____

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 3: Multiples and factors

questions.stem: Write down the first 12 multiples of 4. Then complete a to l. To fill in the blanks, say '1 four is 4', '2 fours are 8', and so on. Count in fours to check your answers. 12 × 4 = ____
questions.hint: Think of 12 groups of 4: skip-count in 4s, 12 times, or use a table you know.

steps.explain: Read the problem as equal groups: 12 rows with 4 in each row (or 12 groups of 4). The total is found by multiplying.

steps.explain: Divide 24 by 5: 5 × 4 = 20, and 24 - 20 = 4. There is a remainder of 4, so 5 does not divide 24 exactly.
Quick test for 5: multiples of 5 end in 0 or 5. 24 ends in 4, so it fails the test.
So 24 is not a multiple of 5.
Why the other answer is wrong: it says the opposite of what the division shows.

questions.stem: The Hayes family bought 42 bananas to share among 6 people. Each person eats 1 banana each day for 1 week. Explain why they bought exactly the right number of bananas.
options: 6 people eat 6 bananas a day, and 6 × 7 days = 42 bananas, so 42 is exactly what they need.
6 + 7 = 13 bananas are needed, so 42 is too many.
42 is an even number, so it is the right number.
Each person eats 42 bananas in a week.
questions.hint: Bananas needed = people × days.

steps.explain: Each person eats 1 banana a day, so the 6 people eat 6 bananas each day.
A week has 7 days, so the family needs 7 groups of 6 bananas.

questions.hint: Each row adds 5 beads, so the total is in the 5 times table.

steps.explain: Each row has 5 beads, so as rows are added the total goes up by 5 each time: 5, 10, 15, ... It is a multiple of 5.

questions.stem: Copy these statements and fill in the blanks. Edna Sharp teaches 8 different music classes. Each class has 3 people in it. This gives a multiple of ____. The total is ____ × ____ = ____ people.
questions.hint: Each class adds 3 people, so the total is in the 3 times table.

steps.explain: Each class has 3 people, so the total goes up by 3 for every class: 3, 6, 9, ... It is a multiple of 3.
There are 8 classes, so the total is 8 × 3.

questions.stem: Copy these statements and fill in the blanks. 28 is the product of ____ and ____.
questions.hint: Find two numbers that multiply to make 28 using your times tables.

steps.explain: 'The product of two numbers' means you MULTIPLY them. We need two numbers that multiply to give 28.
Skip-count or use the times tables: all the pairs that make 28 are 1×28, 2×14, 4×7.
The pair in the question is 4 and 7: 4 × 7 = 28.
Check each other option by multiplying: none of them gives the right product.
Why the other answers are wrong: some add the numbers instead of multiplying; others are only close to the right pair.

keyPoints.note: A product is the answer to a multiplication.

questions.stem: Copy these statements and fill in the blanks by writing 'factor' or 'multiple'. 3 is a ____ of 24 because 24 is a ____ of 3.
questions.hint: The smaller number that divides evenly is the factor; the larger number it divides into is the multiple.

steps.explain: Remember: if a × b = c, then a and b are FACTORS of c, and c is a MULTIPLE of a and of b. The small numbers that multiply are factors; the big product is the multiple.
steps.work: \(a\times b=c\ \Rightarrow\ a,b\ \text{factors of}\ c;\ c\ \text{a multiple of}\ a,b\)

steps.explain: 24 = 8 × 3, so 3 divides 24 exactly: 3 is a factor of 24 and 24 is a multiple of 3.
So the first blank is 'factor' and the second blank is 'multiple'.

Why the other answers are wrong: the two words in a statement of this kind are opposite to each other when the sentence says 'X of Y because Y is a ... of X', so 'factor, factor' and 'multiple, multiple' cannot both be right.

keyPoints.note: A multiple of n is in the n times table (skip-count by n).
n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.

Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 28.

A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.

Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 154.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

meta.source: ICE-EM Mathematics Year 6 (3rd ed.) Chapter 3: Multiples and factors

questions.stem: Find the prime factorisation of these numbers. 7020
questions.hint: Keep splitting off the smallest prime factor (2, 3, 5, ...) until what is left is prime.

steps.explain: Start with 7020 and look for the SMALLEST prime that divides it. Test 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, ... in order.

steps.explain: Write the prime factors in increasing order, joined with ×: this is the prime factorisation.
Check by multiplying the primes together: you must get 7020.

Why the other answers are wrong: one has a factor that is not prime (it can still be split), one has a factor missing (so the product is too small), one has a wrong prime, and one is not in increasing order or has an extra factor.

keyPoints.note: n is a factor of m if m divides by n with nothing left over.
A prime number has exactly two factors: 1 and itself.
Write the number as a product of primes, smallest first.

questions.stem: Write the number that is the product of each prime factorisation. \(2\times3\times5\)
questions.hint: Multiply the primes together one at a time.

steps.explain: Multiply the prime factors together, from left to right.
So the number is 30.
Check: dividing the number by each prime in turn leaves 1 at the end.
Why the other answers are wrong: adding the primes instead of multiplying, or one multiplication slip.
